children.text: A portfolio exists to produce benefits, not deliverables. A completed analytics platform, a certified clinic or a new pricing rule matters only because of what it makes possible: affordable premiums, solvent hospitals, better access, a stronger workforce, narrower gaps. Benefits-realization management is the discipline of tracing each component to the benefits it serves and checking that those benefits actually arrive.

Chapter 15 makes this the Portfolio Manager's core purpose: ensure every component can trace its contribution to one or more of Act 167's five statutory goals, and that the portfolio as a whole produces the benefits that justify its cost. This lesson builds that trace, using the book's benefits-realization plan and PMI's practice guide.

The Transformation Leadership course covers how to sustain benefits after a reform launches. This lesson concentrates on the earlier step: designing the trace from components to goals, choosing the measures, and using it to make portfolio decisions.
Benefits, Not Deliverables

PMI's Benefits Realization Management: A Practice Guide describes benefits realization as the thread that runs from organizational strategy through project deliverables to the benefits they contribute, across portfolio, program and project management. It sets out shared terminology, core principles and a life cycle for identifying, planning, realizing and sustaining benefits.

PMI's own research suggests the discipline is rare. The guide cites the 2018 Pulse of the Profession finding that only one in three organizations report high benefits-realization maturity. Most organizations can say what they delivered; far fewer can say what it achieved.

For a transformation, the gap between delivery and benefit is where reforms quietly fail. A global budget can be implemented on time and still fail to slow cost growth. A medical-home program can reach full coverage and still leave access gaps unchanged. Without a benefits trace, the portfolio will report success on every component while the goals that justified it go unmet.

Benefits also take longer to appear than deliverables, and they are harder to attribute. Premiums respond to many forces besides one pricing rule; access gaps respond to staffing, transport and income as well as to clinical programs. A benefits plan does not need perfect attribution, but it does need agreed measures and agreed expectations about timing, set before results arrive, so that the portfolio is judged against a standard rather than a story.
A deliverable is something the portfolio produces. A benefit is a change in the world the deliverable makes possible. Portfolios are justified by benefits and should be judged by them.
Tracing to Act 167's Five Goals

Vermont's portfolio already has its goals in statute. Act 167 of 2022 set five: high-quality, accessible care; financial sustainability; affordability; a robust workforce; and health equity. Figure 15.8 of the book maps the portfolio's components to each goal, names a measurement metric and sets a 2028 target.

The mapping shows how benefits depend on combinations of components. High-quality, accessible care draws on the Blueprint medical homes, Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics, the HEROI equity methodology and the Care Integration Network. Affordability draws on reference-based pricing and global budgets. Health equity draws on HEROI, health-related social-need screening, social-risk adjustment and social-determinants data. No single component delivers any goal alone, which is why benefits have to be managed at portfolio level.

The targets are concrete enough to check. For accessible care, 90% or better follow-up within 30 days after behavioral-health hospitalization and readmissions below 12%. For affordability, commercial premium growth below 5% a year and total-cost-of-care growth below inflation plus one point. For the workforce, a primary-care staffing gap below 200 full-time equivalents, from 370.

children.text: Choosing Measures: Leading and Lagging

The 2028 targets in Figure 15.8 are lagging indicators: they show whether benefits arrived, but only after the fact. A portfolio office also needs leading indicators that show early whether benefits are on course. For affordability, a leading indicator might be the share of hospital revenue under the new pricing methodology; for equity, the share of hospitals using stratified quality data in their plans.

Leading indicators should be tied to the components that produce the benefit and measured on the portfolio's monthly or quarterly cadence. Lagging indicators are reviewed less often, typically quarterly against the Vermont Scorecard and annually at portfolio rebalancing, which is the cadence the book's roadmap sets.

Equity measures need special care. Chapter 10's principle, calibrate for the gap and not the average, applies here: a portfolio can raise an average while widening a gap. Benefits for equity should therefore be measured as gaps between groups or regions, as Figure 15.8 does with the BIPOC access target and Northeast Kingdom uninsurance, not as statewide averages.

children.text: Using Benefits to Make Portfolio Decisions

The benefits trace is a decision tool. It tells the Portfolio Manager which components are essential to which goals, so that when resources are short the portfolio protects the components on which the most benefit depends. It also reveals goals served by few components, which are more fragile: the workforce goal, for example, depends on a narrow set of investments.

Most importantly, it supports the hardest portfolio decision: stopping work. Chapter 15 gives the Portfolio Manager the duty of tracking benefits realization and recommending that a component be terminated when its benefits are no longer achievable. Without a benefits trace, that judgment cannot be made on evidence, and components continue on momentum.

The trace also connects the portfolio to its overseers. Legislators and boards care about the five goals, not the nineteen components. Reporting progress goal by goal, with the contributing components underneath, gives them the view they need and makes the portfolio's purpose visible in every report.

Benefits also guide sequencing at the margin. When two components compete for the same scarce resource and both are unblocked, the one contributing to more goals, or to a goal with fewer other contributors, usually has the stronger claim. The dependency logic decides what can run; the benefits trace helps decide what should run first among the things that can.

children.text: Build Your Own Benefits Trace

Start from your goals, not your components. Write down the outcomes your transformation exists to achieve, in the form your overseers would recognize: statutory goals, board-approved strategic aims or contractual targets. Then, for each goal, list the components that contribute to it and how.

Every component should appear under at least one goal. A component that serves no goal is a candidate for stopping. A goal with no contributing component is a gap in the portfolio. For each goal, choose one or two lagging measures with a target and date, and one or two leading measures you can track on the portfolio's regular cadence.

Review the trace at each quarterly performance review and at the annual rebalancing. When a benefit is drifting off course, the trace shows which components to examine first; when a component is no longer able to deliver its benefit, the trace supplies the evidence for a decision to stop or redesign it.

Share the trace with the people who run the components. Component leads who can see which goals their work serves make better day-to-day choices, and they are the first to notice when a deliverable is on track but its benefit is not.

body.explanation: Every component should trace to at least one goal. A component that serves none either has an undocumented purpose, which should be made explicit, or is consuming resources without contributing to the portfolio's benefits, which makes it a candidate for termination. Inventing a goal to fit a component reverses the logic of benefits realization.

options.text: Keep it, since it is already in the inventory
Treat it as a candidate for stopping, or find and document the goal it truly serves
Create a new goal so the component has one
